vignette:
Dr. Kwame is twenty years old, a doctor at a hospital in a quiet city in West Africa. He is tall and serious, with hands that move quickly and precisely. When he speaks, he chooses his words carefully, as if each one might weigh too much.

He was seventeen when he first entered the combat zone. Fresh out of medical basics, assigned to a field hospital near the northern border. The war had been on for three years already-artillery, raids, villages burning. His unit treated soldiers and civilians alike. He learned fast.

The event that changed him happened on a Tuesday during the dry season. A convoy of wounded arrived under mortar fire. Kwame was outside the triage tent, directing a litter team, when the air split open. He remembers the sound first-a high thinning whistle that burrowed into his skull-then the pressure wave. He was thrown against a supply truck. His ears rang. Dust filled his throat. When he could see again, the medical tent was gone. The surgical table lay twisted like a strip of metal. A nurse he had worked with that morning was kneeling in the dirt, holding her arm, eyes wide and empty. He remembers running to her, his legs not listening, thinking keep moving keep moving keep moving. He does not remember what he said or did next. He only remembers the boy.

The boy was maybe twelve, a civilian caught in the blast. Kwame found him under the wreckage. He was conscious, asking for water. His legs were gone below the knee, the tissue black and shredded. Kwame tied a tourniquet with his own belt, the boy's blood hot and slick on his fingers. He tried to stabilise him, but the second mortar struck before the evacuation helicopter arrived. The boy died in his arms. Kwame remembers the exact weight of his body, the way his breathing stopped like a door closing.

He was evacuated three days later. Medically cleared. Sent home.

Now he works in a city hospital, emergency department. He is good at his job-fast, calm, precise. But something has shifted. Every time a trauma call comes over the speaker, his chest locks. He sees the dust, the twisted metal, the boy's face. He smells the blood. He has learned to take a step back, close his eyes for one second, then move forward. His colleagues call him disciplined. They do not know he is counting his own breaths.

At night, he cannot sleep. He lies awake in his small apartment, listening to the cars outside, flinching at every backfire. He has stopped going to the market because the crowds feel like a pressure wave. He avoids the smell of diesel and burnt meat. He does not talk about the war. When his mother calls, he says he is fine. When other doctors ask about his northern deployment, he says, "It was difficult," and changes the subject.

He has started wearing his watch on his left wrist, tight, because he once saw a patient lose a hand and the tourniquet was on the left. He does not know why that matters. He only knows that if his watch slides even a little, he feels sick.

Last week, a teenager came in with a leg wound from a machete. Kwame sutured him without trouble. But afterward, in the staff washroom, he stood over the sink and could not stop his hands from shaking. He watched his reflection and thought: You were a doctor before. You are a doctor now. But the reflection did not answer. The boy's face was still there, waiting for water.

He has not told anyone. He goes to work. He comes home. He sits in the dark. The sound of the whistle comes back sometimes-thin, high, endless. He waits for it to stop. It does not.
